items.summary: Replication package for the systematic literature review "Production-Oriented Evaluation and Testing of LLM-Based Agents: A Systematic Literature Review" (revised version, submitted to Information and Software Technology; first submitted as "Evaluation and Testing of LLM-Based Agents in Production: A Systematic Literature Review"). The review follows Kitchenham–Charters guidelines with PRISMA 2020 reporting. The main search covers Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library up to 24 March 2026; with citation tracking it yields a review corpus of 88 primary studies (74 from the main search, 14 from citation tracking). A search extension to 25 September 2026 with the same query and criteria yields 314 further studies, reported as a separate update analysis. A Scopus sensitivity search with broader production-oriented terms (300-record random sample) estimates the recall of the query. Version 2.0.0 accompanies the revised article. Version 1.0.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20583928) accompanies the article as first submitted and is preserved unchanged in the folder 2026-03/. Contents: corpus/, extraction/, risk-of-bias/ — the review corpus of 88: included and excluded studies with screening decisions, dual data extraction (Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2 and arbiter-resolved; 27 analytical fields) and three-domain quality assessment. 2026-03/ — the March 2026 round exactly as released in v1.0.0 (80 studies, agreement reports, audits). 2026-09/ — the September 2026 round: ACM Digital Library and update searches (full-text records R001–R670), Scopus sensitivity search, extraction and quality assessment of 335 studies, agreement reports, and the single-label recode of automated-testing with its held-out validation. primary-studies.bib (88) and 2026-09/primary-studies.bib (335). reproduce.ipynb — a self-contained notebook with 595 automated checks that reproduce every statistic of the article computed from the per-record data (Section 2: review corpus; Section 3: September round; Appendix A: the 2026-03 round as first submitted). README.md (structure, data dictionary, errata), CHANGELOG.md, methodology.md, statistical-analyses.md, prisma-2020-checklist.md, kitchenham-2007-compliance.md, requirements.txt, LICENSE. items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121305 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. Table 2 says the CBT

The data are provided for research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic analysis. Source publications referenced within the dataset remain the property of their respective copyright holders. items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.

items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.

items.summary: Language functions not only as a means of transmitting information but also as a repository of cultural knowledge, collective experience, and culturally shaped patterns of thought. Consequently, translation involves more than the transfer of lexical and grammatical information between languages. It also requires the interpretation and reconstruction of meanings that are embedded within particular cultural contexts. This issue becomes especially evident in the translation of idioms, proverbs, metaphors, realia, and other culture-specific expressions whose meanings cannot always be derived from their individual lexical components. In Translation Studies, such elements are commonly discussed as culture-specific items (CSIs), which may require particular strategies to preserve their semantic, pragmatic, and cultural dimensions in the target language (Aixelá, 1996).
tags: Idiomatic expressions provide a particularly clear illustration of the relationship between language and culture.

items.summary: OWL v1.3.0 This release corrects the free-surface treatment in all 2D and 3D wave solvers and fixes several issues in 3D runs with MPI domain decomposition. Parameter files and output formats are unchanged. Free surface (acoustic, elastic iso/VTI/HTI/ORT, and elastic TTI solvers, 2D and 3D) Wavefield above the surface. The solvers now mirror the particle velocities above the free surface, v(−z) = v(z). Before, the top rows of the finite-difference stencils read zeros there. This made elastic surface amplitudes 6–8% too low at any mesh refinement and caused waveform errors of about 2% in acoustic media. Sources near the surface. A source whose interpolation stencil reaches the surface is injected together with its mirror image. A force is its own image. For an explosion or a moment tensor, the image removes the part that a traction-free surface cannot support. On the refined near-surface mesh, each stencil row is scaled by its own cell height. Before, the solvers dropped the stencil points on and above the surface, and force sources were not normalized by the cell height. In the elastic solvers, a source given above the surface is placed on it; this replaces the former relocation with an empirical amplitude factor. Receivers near the surface. Acoustic receivers whose interpolation stencil reaches above the surface now read the pressure mirrored about it, p(−z) = −p(z). Before, 3D receivers within four grid cells of the surface read zeros there (errors of a few percent), and 2D receivers read a mirror that missed the most recent source injection. FWI near the surface. The adjoint sources follow the same rule as the sources, which makes them the exact adjoint of the receiver sampling. In our tests, source–receiver reciprocity errors near the surface drop from up to 47% to about 10⁻⁵. In 2D acoustic media, the adjoint source no longer accumulates on the surface row, where the pressure must stay zero. The moment-tensor gradient is now the exact transpose of the moment-tensor source, including its mirror image and, in TTI media with topography, the cell scaling of each source column. Accuracy. Against an analytical half-space solution, for explosion, force, and moment-tensor sources at 1.25 m and 20 m depth, amplitudes agree within about 5% at receivers on the surface and within about 2% at 150 m depth (0.2% for the 20 m source). A source exactly on the surface is the worst case: up to about 5% (standard staggered grid) and 10% (fully staggered grid) at the surface receivers with the default 4× refinement. This first-order error halves with each doubling of the refinement. Acoustic results match the exact image solution to about 10⁻⁶. 3D runs with domain decomposition or several shot groups rankx and rankz now decompose the x- and z-axes. Before, they were swapped. FWI without energy preconditioning: the gradient was summed over the blocks of a shot only inside the energy preconditioning, so a decomposed run without it wrote only the block of rank 0. Elastic FWI with a free surface: the gradients of vp, vs, and the anisotropy parameters were zero outside the block of rank 0, because the chain rule took the density from that block only. The solvers now use the input density. FWI: the step length, the merged gradient, and the trace weights now count each shot group once. Before, they counted it once per rank of the group. FWI: the boundary records of the source-wavefield reconstruction are clipped consistently to each block, the restored final-step wavefield gets fresh halos, and halos are refreshed before snapshots and before the gradient computation. The density at force sources (all 3D solvers) and the stability check (TTI) are now reduced over the shot group instead of all ranks. With ngroup > 1, force amplitudes were divided by ngroup and the stable time step was overestimated. Acoustic, free surface: the free-surface flag was read after the domain decomposition, so the first shot of each rank was decomposed as if without a fr

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).

items.summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. items.summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. When a high-confidence correction is found, GradLint can emit repaired FSL and/or MRtrix gradient files together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs.  The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.6, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-03. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).

Contents: the corpus of 144,958 paraphrase pairs (22,053 human-written files in Python, C, C++, Java, C#, Go and PHP, rewritten by Gemini 3 Flash, GPT 5 Nano, Claude 3 Haiku, Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek V3.2, Grok 4 Fast and Devstral 2512 under the paraphrasing instruction of Park et al., 2025), the deterministic fold assignment, the 105-feature matrix, the cross-prompt corpus (the same 1,050 files rewritten under two further instructions), 2,400 human revisions of source files from MIT-licensed repositories (the negative set of the paired detection experiment), the out-of-fold outputs of every view and baseline (tree learners, TF-IDF views, fine-tuned CodeBERT and CodeT5 encoders, attention classifier, LPcodedec replication), every result file behind the article's tables and figures, the Colab notebooks for the GPU baselines, and the scripts that rebuild the corpus, run every experiment and regenerate every table and figure. The human-written files come from public repositories under the MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD 2-Clause and BSD 3-Clause licences and are redistributed under those licences with their notices preserved. Personal markers in identifiers were anonymised. The scripts are released under the MIT licence. The LPcode benchmark and the LPcodedec code of Park et al. are not redistributed; the README documents how to obtain them.

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).

items.summary: Data and Python code accompanying the manuscript “Replication-Based Criteria Can Change the Selected Number of Clusters: A Seven-Criterion Audit of k-Means on Indonesian Provincial Environmental Data” (submitted to the Journal of Computing Theories and Applications). The package audits how the number of clusters, k, is selected for k-means on a small tabular dataset: the published components of Indonesia’s Environmental Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup) for 38 provinces, 2021–2024. Seven criteria are computed for k = 2 to 8: the within-cluster sum of squares (read visually and by two formal knee rules), silhouette width, the Davies–Bouldin and Calinski–Harabasz indices, the gap statistic, subsample stability (adjusted Rand index over 200 pairs of overlapping 80% subsamples) and agreement with Ward linkage. The scripts also run sensitivity analyses, a comparison of six clustering algorithms, fixed-centroid assignment across years, a leave-one-out comparison of regression models for the air quality component, permutation importance and exact Shapley values. Contents: data/ (index components 2021–2024; GRDP per capita and population density; a cell-level provenance audit), code/ (six analysis scripts and a plotting-style module), README.md (run order, variable dictionary and data sources), requirements.txt (pinned library versions), CITATION.cff and licence files. Running the six scripts in the order given in README.md reproduces every table and figure of the manuscript in about four minutes on a laptop (Python 3.11 or later). The indicator values are official statistics from Statistics Indonesia (Badan Pusat Statistik) and are reproduced unchanged. Please cite the original BPS tables as well as this record. Code: MIT licence. Data files: CC BY 4.0.

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Code and text-free reproducibility artifacts for the manuscript “Saudi Arabic Automatic Speech Recognition and Dialect Identification Using Calibrated System Combination and Gated Multimodal Fusion,” currently under revision at Scientific Reports . The repository implements a Saudi Arabic automatic speech recognition framework using XLSR-53, XLS-R 300M, XLS-R 1B, and MMS-1B with validation-tuned KenLM decoding, evaluation under a dialect-normalized scoring convention applied to both references and hypotheses, and calibrated N-best system combination. The reproduced combined test WER is 32.49% , compared with 34.04% for the best single-model configuration. XLSR-53 was evaluated on a 1,652-utterance subset of the test set and is therefore treated as an indicative baseline. The repository also provides SaudiDID-X, a multimodal Saudi dialect identification framework using frozen multi-layer MMS-1B acoustic representations and frozen SaudiBERT text features with a residual adapter and gated fusion. The audio-only comparison is the acoustic branch of the same SaudiDID-X training run , not an independently trained model. The archived test macro-F1 values are 52.01% for the audio-only branch and 53.79% for SaudiDID-X. The release includes analysis and reference-training notebooks, configuration metadata, anonymized split identifiers, text-free per-utterance result artifacts, statistical-test outputs, figures, tables, checksums, and a verification script. Raw audio and third-party transcriptions are not redistributed because of source-specific licensing restrictions. v1.0.2: Documentation, provenance, and configuration-metadata corrections. Archived predictions, primary reported metrics, data splits, checksums, and computational implementation are unchanged. See CHANGELOG.md for the complete list of corrections. v1.0.1: Configuration-metadata corrections for the single-run reporting protocol and per-stage training hyperparameters. No result values changed.
items.title: SaudiArabic-ASR-DID: Multi-Model ASR and Multimodal Dialect Identification for Saudi Arabic

items.summary: This dataset contains the experimental materials and retained research records supporting the master’s thesis on evaluating LLM-based identification of non-functional requirements (NFRs) from agile user stories. The dataset consists of two Excel files: Research_Experiment_Data_Final.xlsx This file contains the retained experimental records used in the study, including: reconstructed user stories and their provenance; human analyst NFR annotations; consensus voting and the resulting baseline NFRs; AI-generated NFR identification results from repeated GPT-4o-mini runs; AI consistency results across repeated runs; AI-human matching and adjudication results; timing observations for human and AI-based NFR identification; System Usability Scale (SUS) responses; per-evaluator and aggregate performance metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score. 25_reconstructed_stories_.xlsx This file contains the 25 reconstructed user stories used as the experimental input dataset. It documents the source material used for reconstruction, source URLs, source evidence, the rationale for reconstruction, and the resulting reconstructed user stories. The reconstructed stories were created for the experiment and should not be interpreted as verbatim quotations of the original source datasets. Together, these files provide the underlying experimental records and input materials necessary to understand and reproduce the quantitative analyses reported in the thesis. The dataset supports examination of human versus LLM-based NFR identification, including identification accuracy, consistency, agreement with the human-derived baseline, processing time, and usability. The data are provided for research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic analysis. Source publications referenced within the dataset remain the property of their respective copyright holders. The reconstructed user stories are experimental research materials derived from source-supported characteristics and are explicitly documented as reconstructed rather than presented as original source text.
items.title: LLM-Based NFR Identification: Experimental Dataset

items.summary: Privacy-derived scientific materials for controlled studies of evidence access and adverse product content in AI assessment. The supplement contains synthetic materials, prompts, recorded model answers, terminal failures, assignment mappings, original stage-specific scoring and statistical implementations, reference results, and an offline CPU replay entrypoint. It includes the main local studies, the hosted-model study, historical screening, two common-interface qualification rounds, and the exploratory two-model pilot. Screening and development records are kept distinct from formal comparisons; reused answer aliases are not independent generations. The qualification amendment was made after qualification and before the exploratory pilot, and the subsequent proposed formal extension was not run. The findings do not establish a general advantage of pre-event defense, equivalence, or broad robustness. This is a redacted scientific derivative with a new integrity manifest: account authorizations, user dialogue, machine paths, hardware logs, original provider envelopes, encrypted reasoning, native token journals and model weights are excluded. CPU replay reproduces scores and statistics from the released scientific records; it does not regenerate answers or repeat the original private token/authorization/environment audits.
items.title: Scientific supplement for Evidence Access and Adverse Product Content in AI Assessment

items.summary: gpbiometricspy is the Python counterpart of gpbiometrics, with gpbiometrics 2.0.0 frozen as its initial semantic reference. It provides Gazepoint-native workflows for EDA/GSR/SCR, PPG/HRV, pupil, gaze, fixation, AOI, TTL/event alignment, multimodal quality control, analysis, plotting, reporting, simulation, reproducibility, and interoperability. Version 0.1.8 preserves the complete 406-export scientific contract, freezes 874 passing exact-main tests and 15,612/15,612 covered statements, retains 7,315/7,334 = 99.7409% raw branch coverage with exactly 19 reviewed residual arcs and zero unexpected, stale, or unaudited branch debt, and adds the Python-native PPG pigmentation / measurement-equity audit with deterministic synthetic evidence plus an authorized STEP wearable-heart-rate execution. STEP Fitzpatrick phototype is treated as subjective categorical provenance only; ENCoDE remains deferred and no clinical SpO2 validation is claimed.
items.title: gpbiometricspy: Python tools for Gazepoint biometric workflows

items.summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript ‘PCMTL: Physics-Consistent and Uncertainty-Calibrated Multi-Task Learning for Trustworthy Multi-Property Polymer Screening’. It contains source code, frozen configurations, controlled software-verification fixtures and outputs, figures, manuscript and Supplementary files, environment specifications, licenses, and a provenance manifest for external production data. The bundled verification fixtures and verification outputs are deterministic software-verification assets and are not real polymer-discovery results. Production material-level claims require the external PolyOmics and PI1M resources listed in DATA_MANIFEST.csv and execution of python reproduce.py --config configs/main.yaml
items.title: PCMTL: Reproducibility Archive for Physics-Consistent, Uncertainty-Calibrated Polymer Screening.

items.summary: This dataset contains the derived summary resources supporting the manuscript Sequence-to-function models prioritize fine-mapped blood eQTLs in African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic White participants . The package includes the source tables for every main and supplementary figure and table, model-score summaries, fine-mapping benchmark tables, AUROC resampling summaries, the matched FILER functional-annotation enrichment analysis (inputs, results, and QC), the follow-up analyses that dissect the group difference (score anatomy, resampling, LD, allele frequency, label transfer, within-gene evaluation, annotation baselines), the model-first LD-reduced evaluation (configuration, results, and QC), the eQTLGen replication summary, and row-level prediction tables. The package is split into several archives; the top-level README and MANIFEST describe every file and how the archives fit together. No individual-level genotypes or sample identifiers are included. Analysis code for model scoring, summary analyses, and manuscript figure and table generation is available at https://github.com/Xinyu-Sun/s2f_snp_eqtl_analysis_code, commit b5a9e1270f431a82265d63f0b90ee17eabb9da6c. Version 2026-10-03.
items.title: Data package for evaluating sequence-to-function deep learning models for ancestry-stratified regulatory variant effect prediction

items.summary: Reviewer reproducibility materials for the manuscript Historical Window Choice and Forecast Horizon in Road Traffic Forecasting: Evidence from Great Britain, 1976–2025. This package contains the frozen analytical data, preserved source code, protocol and audit documents, archived numerical outputs, reviewer-facing reproduction scripts, validation files, and checksums used to support the reported analyses. The package also includes documented post-hoc sensitivity analyses, uncertainty reporting, simulation checks, provenance records, and reproducibility validations. Historical protocol and addendum files are retained in their original form to preserve the chronological audit trail. This version aligns the repository metadata with the final manuscript title and incorporates the manuscript’s latest transparency and reporting updates, including the fixed-target 2017–2025 interval-coverage table derived from previously archived target-level outputs. The archived materials are provided to support independent verification of the study’s methods, calculations, reported numerical results, and analytical workflo
